newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stock rally seen unlikely to warm H share chill.
newsitem.headline: HK stock rally seen unlikely to warm H share chill.

text.p: The recent rally in Hong Kong stocks and China's B share markets has sparked hopes that "H" shares may emerge from the doldrums, but analysts said structual problems were still plaguing these Chinese firms.
H shares are Hong Kong-listed shares of state-owned mainland Chinese companies.
"I think it's going to be a little while before the H shares experience any of the enthusiasm," said Alex Conroy, senior China analyst of ING Barings.

While the blue chip Hang Seng Index scored a record close on Wednesday, rising 45.62 points to 13,530.95, the H share index eased 5.47 points to 810.45. The Hang Seng is up 34 percent this year but the H share index has only advanced seven percent.
Percy Au-Young, research director at DBS Securities, also saw no immediate signs that the H shares could break out of their consolidation.
"We still can't see any confirmation that the H share index will reverse its current bearish trend," he said.
Analysts said the problem with the H share companies, mostly involved in heavy industry, was structural. Earnings prospects were dull due to their highly cyclical and rigid characteristics.

Conroy said most people looking for China-related stocks probably would continue in the short term to focus on red chips, Hong Kong companies in China-focussed businesses, which have been active recently in pursuing acqusitions and spin-offs.
"There is quite a bit of activity by the red chips because of the ways red chips work, because of the ways they grow. There is a lot more excitement about them right now," she said.
Each acquisition could have big growth potential and provide an immediate boost to earnings, while the earnings profile for many H shares was predictable.
Andrew Kuet, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said H shares were unlikely to stage a major rally until there was proof that their operating environment had improved.
"Many of the state-owned companies in China are still in shortage of funds and employees are underworked," he said.
DBS's Au-Young also said the crux of the problem for China's state-owned companies was the growing foreign competition introduced by China's open door policy.
"The companies are still in a stage of correction and adjustment in order to adapt to the changing market," he said.
Previous poor earnings from many H share companies have left investors shocked and very cautious about the sector.

"I think major funds are sort of reducing their holdings by the end of this year just to show to their customers that they don't hold H shares," said Henry Lui, research analyst at Mansion House Research.
Au-Young also said he believed most investors would continue to take a wait-and-see attitude in the next three to six months.
"Of course more positive sentiment would help, but the bigger driver would be changes in the fundamentals," added Conroy.
